screens.title: Iterator Pattern: Traversing Collections
screens.subtitle: Access sequence without exposing structure — the .NET way with IEnumerable and IEnumerator

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn why the Iterator pattern exists and how C# exposes it through IEnumerable and IEnumerator. We will ground the idea with a concrete custom collection example and show how foreach translates into enumerator calls. Knowing this pattern helps you decouple traversal logic from storage, so a collection can change implementation without breaking client code. You will see how to implement a custom aggregate and iterator, how MoveNext and Current work, and why disposing iterators matters when they hold resources. We'll also cover common pitfalls such as exposing internal lists and the dangers of modifying a collection while it's being enumerated. By the end you'll be able to write a Playlist or Menu that supports foreach and LINQ and understand when to provide multiple traversal strategies like reverse or filtered iterators. As you explore, keep in mind the practical benefit: clean separation of concerns and flexible traversal strategies that make your collections robust and compatible with. NET language features. Consider this a guide to make your custom data structures first-class citizens in C#.

screens.title: What the Iterator pattern solves
screens.subtitle: A clear definition, a real-world metaphor, and why it matters

narration.text: The Iterator pattern defines a way to access elements of a collection sequentially without revealing how the collection is stored. Put plainly, it gives you a controlled 'walk' through an aggregate. Imagine a playlist: a user wants to play each song in order, but should not be tied to whether songs are stored in an array, list, or a more complex structure. If you expose your storage directly, client code becomes coupled to that choice. The Iterator pattern splits responsibilities: the aggregate manages storage and life cycle; the iterator encapsulates traversal. In C#, IEnumerable is the aggregate interface and IEnumerator is the iterator interface. A common misconception is that foreach hides complexity; while true, foreach relies on the iterator contract, so you still must supply a correct enumerator for custom collections. A concrete example is a Menu class returning a DinerMenuIterator that steps across an internal array and checks for null slots. The takeaway: when you design a custom collection, prefer an iterator interface so callers use a stable traversal A P I; ask yourself, can I change storage later without rewriting client code?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Iterator separates traversal from storage so clients can iterate without depending on an aggregate's internal representation.

content.html:
Core Concept › What the Iterator pattern solves
Pattern definition and metaphor
Iterate without exposing how the collection stores items. Think: a playlist you can walk through regardless of internal storage.
  • • Problem: clients tied to internal representation if you expose storage directly.
  • • Claim: provide an Iterator object to step through elements instead of exposing the collection.
  • • Misconception: foreach removes the need to implement iterators — it only hides the calls; you must implement enumerators for custom collections.
Key Takeaway

Design traversal as a separate component so collection internals can change without impacting callers.

Concrete example: Menu and MenuItem
A DinerMenu holds MenuItem objects in an array. DinerMenu exposes GetEnumerator which returns a DinerMenuIterator that knows how to step through the array and skip nulls.
Analogy
Iterator is like a bookmark in a book — it remembers your current position while the book stays unchanged.
Common mistake
Returning the internal list directly couples callers to implementation and prevents changing storage later.

screens.title: Iterator, Concrete Iterator, Aggregate, Concrete Aggregate
screens.subtitle: Map pattern roles to IEnumerable and IEnumerator in C#

narration.text: The Iterator pattern is expressed as four roles. First, the Iterator interface defines traversal operations: check for more elements and retrieve the current one. In. NET this is IEnumerator, which exposes Current, MoveNext, and Reset. Second, the Concrete Iterator implements IEnumerator and keeps traversal state such as the current index. In our example DinerMenuIterator tracks a position and checks for nulls while moving. Third, the Aggregate interface declares a method to create an iterator. In. NET the Aggregate is IEnumerable, which has GetEnumerator. Fourth, the Concrete Aggregate implements IEnumerable and returns a Concrete Iterator instance from GetEnumerator. A common confusion is thinking the aggregate must perform traversal; it must not. The aggregate's job is to manage items and create iterators on demand. A concrete example: DinerMenu implements IEnumerable and returns new DinerMenuIterator(_menuItems). If you need multiple traversal algorithms, supply different iterator classes and factory methods such as GetReverseEnumerator or GetVegetarianEnumerator. This separation keeps traversal logic testable and replaceable. Iterator, Concrete Iterator, Aggregate, Concrete Aggregate means ienumerable<t> is the aggregate interface; ienumerator<t> is the iterator interface. concrete classes implement these roles separately.. In practical terms, map pattern roles to ienumerable and ienumerator in c#. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Component Mapping
keyIdea.text: IEnumerable<T> is the Aggregate interface; IEnumerator<T> is the Iterator interface. Concrete classes implement these roles separately.

content.html:
Pattern Components › Iterator Roles
Iterator (IEnumerator<T>)
Defines MoveNext(), Current, Reset(). It encapsulates traversal state and rules.
Concrete Iterator
Implements IEnumerator<T>, tracks position, handles sparse arrays or traversal variations.
Aggregate (IEnumerable<T>)
Declares GetEnumerator which returns an IEnumerator<T> to clients.
Concrete Aggregate
Implements IEnumerable<T> and returns instances of concrete iterators. Keeps storage private.
Example mapping
DinerMenu : IEnumerable<MenuItem> → GetEnumerator() returns DinerMenuIterator : IEnumerator<MenuItem>.
Pro tip
If you need multiple traversals, offer named factory methods that return different concrete iterators instead of embedding traversal logic in the aggregate.

screens.title: DinerMenu and DinerMenuIterator example
screens.subtitle: A guided review of the sample C# implementation

narration.text: Let's walk through the DinerMenu example step by step. The MenuItem type is a simple element with Name, Price, and a Print method. DinerMenu is the concrete aggregate that stores MenuItem instances in a fixed-size array and implements IEnumerable. Its GetEnumerator returns a new DinerMenuIterator constructed with the internal array. DinerMenuIterator implements IEnumerator. It keeps a private int position starting at -1. MoveNext increments the position and returns true when the element exists and is non-null; Current returns the element at the current position or throws if out of range. Reset brings the position back to -1 and Dispose is present for resource cleanup. A crucial detail: MoveNext checks for null to handle sparse arrays. A common misconception is to trust internal collections to never change; production iterators often include a version check to detect concurrent modification and throw a clear exception. This example shows separation of responsibilities: DinerMenu manages items; the iterator manages stepping logic. Ask yourself: if storage changes, which class must change? The aggregate will change storage, but existing iterator implementations keep traversal rules isolated. DinerMenu and DinerMenuIterator example means concrete iterator maintains traversal state; aggregate returns it. movenext and current coordinate to present a safe sequence to callers.. In practical terms, a guided review of the sample c# implementation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Code Insight
keyIdea.text: Concrete iterator maintains traversal state; aggregate returns it. MoveNext and Current coordinate to present a safe sequence to callers.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › DinerMenu example
Key excerpt (iterator core)
public class DinerMenuIterator : IEnumerator<MenuItem>
{
  private MenuItem[] _list;
  private int _position = -1;

  public DinerMenuIterator(MenuItem[] list)
  {
    _list = list;
  }

  public MenuItem Current
  {
    get
    {
      try
      {
        return _list[_position];
      }
      catch (IndexOutOfRangeException)
      {
        throw new InvalidOperationException();
      }
    }
  }

  object IEnumerator.Current => Current;

  public bool MoveNext()
  {
    _position++;
    return (_position < _list.Length && _list[_position] != null);
  }

  public void Reset() { _position = -1; }
  public void Dispose() { }
}
Explanation
Position starts before first element. MoveNext advances and returns whether a valid element exists. Current reads the element or raises if invalid.
Concrete example
DinerMenu constructs a DinerMenuIterator with its internal array; foreach uses that iterator under the hood.
Misconception
Assuming MoveNext will skip removed items safely — concurrent modification may cause exceptions unless guarded.

screens.title: How to implement IEnumerable & IEnumerator in C#
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step recipe to make a custom collection enumerable

narration.text: Implementing enumeration in C# follows a reliable sequence. Step one: choose your internal storage; the DinerMenu used an array but you can use a List. Step two: implement the Aggregate by making your collection implement IEnumerable and add GetEnumerator that returns a concrete iterator. Step three: implement a Concrete Iterator class that implements IEnumerator. It needs a constructor that accepts your storage, a Current property that returns the current element, MoveNext that advances the position and returns whether an element is available, Reset to reposition to the start, and Dispose to release any resources. Step four: implement the non-generic IEnumerable and IEnumerator explicit members if you want backward compatibility with old APIs; usually these just call the generic members. A practical gotcha: MoveNext must handle sparse collections and not assume contiguous storage. Another is disposal: if your iterator wraps a stream or database cursor, Dispose must close it. After these steps your collection supports foreach and works with LINQ operators, which rely on the iterator contract. Process Flow › Implementing IEnumerable/IEnumerator
Steps
  1. 1. Choose storage: Array or List are common. Keep storage private.
  2. 2. Implement IEnumerable<T>: Add public IEnumerator<T> GetEnumerator() returning a new iterator.
  3. 3. Create IEnumerator<T>: Implement Current, MoveNext, Reset, Dispose and a constructor that receives storage.
  4. 4. Add non-generic compatibility: Implement IEnumerator and IEnumerable explicit members by delegating.
  5. 5. Safety: Handle nulls, sparse arrays, and call Dispose when needed.
Follow these steps and the collection will integrate with foreach and LINQ automatically.
Example method
GetEnumerator returns new ConcreteIterator(_storage). Keep this factory logic simple and focused.

Common mistake

screens.title: foreach vs manual enumerator usage
screens.subtitle: How foreach maps to GetEnumerator, MoveNext, and Current

narration.text: In C#, the foreach loop is a language surface that relies on the iterator contract. When you write foreach over a collection the compiler generates calls to GetEnumerator(), then repeatedly calls MoveNext() and accesses Current until MoveNext returns false, finally disposing the enumerator if needed. Manually using IEnumerator requires the same steps written explicitly, which is helpful when you need fine-grained control—for example, when filtering as you step through items or when you need to Dispose early. The benefit of foreach is readability and safety: it ensures disposal in a finally block. A common misconception is that manual iteration is always inefficient; it can be necessary when you want to pause iteration, maintain a long-lived enumerator, or implement custom filtering without creating intermediate collections. A concrete example: you can write a while loop that calls MoveNext and checks Current. IsVegetarian to print only vegetarian items. Remember to call Dispose on manual enumerators or wrap them in a using pattern to avoid resource leaks if the iterator holds resources. foreach vs manual enumerator usage means foreach is syntactic sugar for enumerator calls; use manual enumerators only when you need explicit control or resource management.. In practical terms, how foreach maps to getenumerator, movenext, and current. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Iteration Styles
keyIdea.text: foreach is syntactic sugar for enumerator calls; use manual enumerators only when you need explicit control or resource management.

content.html:
Comparison › foreach vs manual enumerator
foreach (compiler-generated)
Compiler calls GetEnumerator, then MoveNext/Current in a loop and disposes the enumerator automatically.
• Safer for resource disposal.
• Cleaner and preferred for simple traversal.
Manual IEnumerator
You call GetEnumerator(), then loop with MoveNext and use Current, and call Dispose when finished.
• Use when you need control or to pause iteration.
• Must manage Dispose to avoid leaks when iterators hold resources.
Concrete example
Manual enumeration filters vegetarian items by checking Current.IsVegetarian inside a while loop using MoveNext.
Misconception
Thinking foreach removes the need to implement IEnumerable; you still must provide a correct enumerator for custom collections.

screens.title: Supporting multiple traversal algorithms
screens.subtitle: Provide different concrete iterators instead of embedding traversal logic

narration.text: Often a single collection logically supports several traversal orders. For a list you might want forward and reverse; for a menu you might offer a vegetarian-only traversal; for a tree you might offer pre-order, in-order, and post-order. The Iterator pattern supports this by letting you implement multiple Concrete Iterators. Instead of adding many traversal methods to the aggregate you can provide factory methods that return different iterator objects, such as GetReverseEnumerator or GetVegetarianEnumerator. Each iterator encapsulates its own traversal algorithm and keeps the collection class focused on storage and management. A common pitfall is to add traversal logic to the aggregate which violates Single Responsibility and bloats the collection. A concrete example from the chapter: you could implement VegetarianMenuIterator that wraps the same storage but skips non-vegetarian items in MoveNext. This approach makes traversals composable, testable, and easy to extend without modifying existing client code. Ask: does adding a traversal change the aggregate's responsibility? If so, prefer a new Concrete Iterator. Supporting multiple traversal algorithms means add new concrete iterators for different traversal algorithms instead of embedding traversal methods in the aggregate.. In practical terms, provide different concrete iterators instead of embedding traversal logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Multiple Traversals
keyIdea.text: Add new Concrete Iterators for different traversal algorithms instead of embedding traversal methods in the aggregate.

content.html:
Process › Traversal strategies
Forward iterator
Standard left-to-right traversal using an index or cursor.
Reverse iterator
Starts at the end and decrements the position. Expose as GetReverseEnumerator.
Filtered iterator
Skips items that don't meet criteria, such as a VegetarianMenuIterator that only returns vegetarian items.
Design rule
Prefer separate iterator types for each traversal algorithm. This keeps traversal logic independent and easily testable.

screens.title: Concurrent modification and safe iteration
screens.subtitle: Why modifying a collection while iterating is dangerous and how to handle it

narration.text: A frequent runtime problem is concurrent modification: changing the underlying collection while an enumerator is active. Many enumerable implementations maintain an internal version or modification count. If the collection is modified during enumeration, the iterator detects the mismatch and throws an InvalidOperationException to prevent unpredictable behavior. Our simple array-based iterator might not check versions, but production iterators often do. To work safely, either avoid structural modifications while iterating or use safe strategies: iterate over a copy, collect items to remove and perform removals after enumeration, or use index-based reverse iteration for removal when appropriate. Another option is providing special iterators that can tolerate changes by snapshotting state. Also remember to Dispose enumerators if they wrap external resources. A common misconception is that small modifications are harmless; even a single removal may invalidate indexes and lead to missed elements or exceptions. The takeaway: design for safe iteration by choosing a strategy up front and document whether your collection supports concurrent modification during enumeration. Concurrent modification and safe iteration means modifying a collection while enumerating can throw exceptions or cause unpredictable results; prefer safe removal strategies or version checks.. In practical terms, why modifying a collection while iterating is dangerous and how to handle it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Concurrent Modification
keyIdea.text: Modifying a collection while enumerating can throw exceptions or cause unpredictable results; prefer safe removal strategies or version checks.

content.html:
Warning › Concurrent modification
What happens
Enumerators often carry a version stamp. If the collection's version changes during iteration the enumerator detects the mismatch and throws an InvalidOperationException.
• Safe removal strategies: iterate a copy, collect removals then remove after enumeration, or use a reverse index loop for indexed collections.
• Snapshot iterators take a copy of elements at the start to avoid mid-iteration changes but cost memory.
• Always Dispose enumerators that wrap resources.
Quick checklist
  • • Will callers modify during enumeration?
  • • Do iterators check a version stamp?
  • • Is snapshotting acceptable for your scenario?

screens.title: Making iterators robust and .NET-friendly
screens.subtitle: Design patterns, disposal, LINQ compatibility, and testing advice

narration.text: When designing iterators for. NET, aim for robustness and ecosystem compatibility. Implement IDisposable on iterators that hold unmanaged resources and ensure GetEnumerator returns a fresh iterator for each call. Favor returning IEnumerable from your collection so LINQ operators work seamlessly. Write unit tests that iterate over empty, full, and sparse collections, and test behavior when MoveNext reaches the end and when Reset is called. For collections that might change, decide on a policy: version checks to throw on modification, snapshot iterators that freeze the sequence at creation, or documented unsupported concurrent modification. Use multiple concrete iterators to support alternate traversals rather than adding traversal methods to the aggregate. A practical example: implement VegetarianMenuIterator for filtered traversal so client code can simply foreach over the vegetarian view. Finally, document disposal expectations and whether enumerators are single-use. The key takeaway: treat traversal as a first-class capability of your collection and make it safe and predictable for callers and LINQ consumers. Making iterators robust and .NET-friendly means return fresh iterators, implement dispose when needed, test edge cases, and document concurrent modification policies.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Return fresh iterators, implement Dispose when needed, test edge cases, and document concurrent modification policies.

Best Practices › Robust iterator design
Disposal
Implement Dispose for iterators that manage external resources and ensure using patterns or foreach properly disposes them.
LINQ compatibility
Expose IEnumerable<T> so your collection works with LINQ operators without extra adapters.
Testing
Unit test empty, single, sparse, and concurrent modification scenarios to validate iterator behavior.
Final checklist
Return fresh iterators, document modification policies, implement Dispose if needed, and provide specialized iterators for alternate traversals.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the essential ideas to carry forward. First: the Iterator pattern separates traversal from storage; use IEnumerable and IEnumerator so clients traverse without seeing your internal representation. Second: implement concrete iterators for each traversal algorithm rather than stuffing traversal logic into the aggregate; this keeps responsibilities clear and code testable. Third: be mindful of concurrent modification and resource management; either detect and fail fast with version checks, snapshot the sequence, or document safe removal strategies, and implement Dispose when your iterator wraps external resources. These three practices make custom collections predictable, compatible with foreach and LINQ, and ready for real-world use. keyIdea.text: IEnumerable => GetEnumerator, IEnumerator => MoveNext/Current/Reset, Dispose when needed, test iteration edge cases.

content.html:
Key Concepts › Quick Reference
IEnumerable / IEnumerator
Aggregate declares GetEnumerator; iterator provides MoveNext and Current.
Dispose and resources
Always Dispose enumerators that wrap streams or external handles.
Test edge cases
Verify empty, sparse, and concurrent modification behaviors with unit tests.
Final Tip

If you need custom traversals, provide additional concrete iterators rather than adding traversal responsibilities to the collection itself.
